::: {#case .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-case">
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">1 · The puzzle</p><p>A large new load, such as a data center or a factory, is ready to run, but its grid service will not start for months. What does the wait cost, and who pays?</p><p class="lx-hint">Words first: <span class="lx-term" data-term="energization">energization</span> is switching on grid service; the <span class="lx-term" data-term="developer">developer</span> is the company building the facility; <span class="lx-term" data-term="ratepayer">ratepayers</span> are the utility's other customers.</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">2 · The question in one sentence</p><p class="lx-case-q">What does it cost when a large data center must wait for grid <span class="lx-term" data-term="energization">energization</span>, and how does the delay affect the developer, electricity ratepayers and society?</p><p class="lx-hint">Question type: descriptive (how much, and for whom?).</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">3 · Scale and boundary</p><ul><li><b>Inside:</b> one large load waiting for its first grid service (the study's case: a 300 <span class="lx-term" data-term="mw-it">MW-IT</span> data center), priced for three parties in <span class="lx-term" data-term="present-value">present value</span>.</li><li><b>Left out:</b> why the connection is late, whether the network can carry the load, and real project data: the parameters are illustrative.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">4 · Decisions, goal and rules, in words</p><ul><li><b>Decisions:</b> whether to pay for a mitigation option (<span class="lx-term" data-term="staged-energization">staged service</span> or <span class="lx-term" data-term="bridge-power">bridge power</span>), and who funds it.</li><li><b>Goal:</b> price the wait for each party, so an option can be judged against what it saves each one.</li><li><b>Rules:</b> the three accounts stay separate; a <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-benefit-test">net-benefit test</span> says when they may be combined.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">5 · Data and method</p><ul><li>A present-value framework turns the delayed computing capacity into the grid MW it needs and prices the delay in three ledgers.</li><li>Two measures compare cases: a delay cost per MW-month, and the largest payment worth making to shorten the wait.</li><li>Inputs are screened with <span class="lx-term" data-term="latin-hypercube">Latin hypercube sampling</span>.</li></ul></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">6 · What came out, and where it holds</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:code"><p>A late grid connection costs the developer lost <span class="lx-term" data-term="margin">margin</span> and <span class="lx-term" data-term="carrying-cost">carrying costs</span>; ratepayers face utility carrying and <span class="lx-term" data-term="stranded-cost">stranding</span> costs; society bears <span class="lx-term" data-term="external-cost">external costs</span>.</p><p>The study keeps these present-value accounts separate.</p><p>For a 300 MW-IT facility, a 36-month delay costs the developer on the order of $0.7 billion in present value.</p><p>Staged energization can recover a large share of that cost.</p><p>Ratepayer exposure depends strongly on large-load <span class="lx-term" data-term="tariff">tariff</span> design.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2026), accepted paper, 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS); DOI pending.</footer></blockquote>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:code"><p>The delay is treated as <span class="lx-term" data-term="exogenous">exogenous</span> and parameters are illustrative; network feasibility is not modeled, and the social perspective is illustrated with a single bridge-power example.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2026), accepted paper, 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS); DOI pending.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">Holds when: the delay is given and the inputs are illustrative. Leaves out: why service is late.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf7" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf7-cost-of-waiting.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The question in time</p>
<!-- cf7-timeline:start (written from the data file by LX.Timeline's staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->

## The idea behind it, then where the result holds
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="cf7-idea" data-src="../assets/learn/data/cf7-cost-of-waiting.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- cf7-idea:start (written from the toy model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">One large load waits for the grid (illustrative)</p><table class="lx-facts cf7-assume"><caption class="lx-hint">The toy's assumptions (illustrative)</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">The load</th><td>100 MW, such as a data center or a factory</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Margin once connected</th><td>$45,000 per MW a month (revenue minus operating costs)</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Capital ready and idle</th><td>$500M of buildings and equipment, carried at the discount rate</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Grid upgrades built for it</th><td>$60M; while it waits, the utility's money in them still costs interest</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Chance it never arrives</th><td>0.5% more each month of waiting, at most 50%; then the upgrades are stranded</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Large-load tariff</th><td>decides what share of those utility costs the waiting load pays; other customers pay the rest</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Bridge power</th><td>on-site generators run half the load during the wait, at $30 per MWh above grid power</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Its CO₂</th><td>0.1 t per MWh more than grid power, had the load been connected on time; $100 per tonne</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Discounting</th><td>8% a year, month by month</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="lx-hint">Worked month: the lost margin is $45,000 × 100 MW = $4.5M a month. Over 24 months, discounted month by month, that is $4.5M × 22.17 = $99.8M today.</p><table class="lx-facts"><caption class="lx-hint">Present values of a 100 MW load's wait, other customers paying the utility's costs, no bridge power.</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Wait</th><th scope="col">Developer</th><th scope="col">Other customers</th><th scope="col">Society</th><th scope="col">Developer per MW-month</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>6 months</td><td class="n">$45.3M</td><td class="n">$4.0M</td><td class="n">$0.0M</td><td class="n">$75.5k</td></tr><tr><td>18 months</td><td class="n">$130.8M</td><td class="n">$11.4M</td><td class="n">$0.0M</td><td class="n">$72.6k</td></tr><tr><td>30 months</td><td class="n">$209.9M</td><td class="n">$17.9M</td><td class="n">$0.0M</td><td class="n">$70.0k</td></tr><tr><td>42 months</td><td class="n">$283.2M</td><td class="n">$23.8M</td><td class="n">$0.0M</td><td class="n">$67.4k</td></tr></tbody></table><ul><li>At 24 months, a tariff that makes the waiting load pay all of the utility's costs moves $14.7M from other customers to the developer; the total stays $185.8M.</li><li>Bridge power for half the load saves the developer $25.6M and adds $8.1M of CO₂ damage above grid power, for society.</li></ul>
<!-- cf7-idea:end -->
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Three accounts, three questions</h3></header>
<table class="cf-two">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Account</th><th scope="col">What the wait costs them</th><th scope="col">The question it answers</th><th scope="col">In the toy, 24 months, no tariff</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><th scope="row">Developer (private)</th><td data-l="What the wait costs them">margin not earned; interest on buildings and equipment that sit idle</td><td data-l="The question it answers">Is shortening the wait worth paying for?</td><td data-l="In the toy, 24 months">$171.1M</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row">Other customers (<span class="lx-term" data-term="ratepayer">ratepayers</span>)</th><td data-l="What the wait costs them">the utility's carrying cost of upgrades built for the load, and the risk they are stranded</td><td data-l="The question it answers">Does the tariff protect people who did not ask for the load?</td><td data-l="In the toy, 24 months">$14.7M</td></tr>
<tr><th scope="row">Society</th><td data-l="What the wait costs them">external costs, such as bridge power's CO₂ above what grid power would have emitted</td><td data-l="The question it answers">Does an option add harm that nobody pays for?</td><td data-l="In the toy, 24 months">$0.0M</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p class="lx-hint">One total would hide who pays.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">In this toy, a tariff only moves a fixed cost between accounts; it does not change the wait or what anyone does. Only a shorter wait shrinks the cost.</p>
</div>

<div class="lx-fallback">

(2026), NAPS 2026 (accepted).</p>

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Present value month by month, and the most worth paying to wait less</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- A cost $c$ in each month of a $\tau$-month wait is worth $c \cdot \frac{1 - (1+i)^{-\tau}}{i}$ today, with $i = (1+r)^{1/12} - 1$ the monthly rate for a yearly [discount rate]{.lx-term term="discount-rate"} $r$ ([lesson 7](07-cost.html) discounts by the year).
- The most a developer should pay to shorten the wait is the cost it avoids: its cost at the original wait minus its cost at the shorter one, before other risks or costs.
- In the toy, 24 → 18 months avoids $40.3M ($171.1M − $130.8M).
- An option creates an overall net benefit when the savings in all accounts exceed its cost plus any harm it adds, each counted once.
- Making every party better off may also take compensation; who pays is a separate choice.
- Sampling uncertain inputs comes in Scenarios, Monte Carlo and global sensitivity (M7, upcoming); why connections take years, in A6 (upcoming).

```{=html}

## Check yourself, then try it
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="cf7-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="tariff" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A tariff that makes the waiting load pay the utility's costs makes the delay cheaper.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In the toy at 24 months it moves $14.7M from other customers to the developer; the total stays $185.8M.</p><p>In this toy, the tariff only reallocates a fixed cost; it does not change the wait or what anyone does.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bridge" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An option can save the developer money while adding a cost that someone else bears.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. In the toy at 24 months, bridge power for half the load saves the developer $25.6M and adds $8.1M of CO₂ damage above grid power. Separate accounts show both.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes; needs Python on your computer (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<ul>
<li>Run <code>examples/minimal.py</code>. Write the illustrative files with <code>code-delay example my_scenario.json --grid grid.json --ranges ranges.json</code>.</li>
<li>Double <code>delay_months</code> in <code>my_scenario.json</code> and run <code>code-delay run my_scenario.json --out-dir outputs/run</code>. Does the developer's cost per MW-month stay level?</li>
<li>Run <code>examples/options.py</code>: compare staged service with full service, and read the net-benefit test for the bridge pathway.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/code-delayed-energization">code-delayed-energization</a>: public example repository · MIT licence · illustrative inputs.</p>
</div>
